adds.title: U.S. Supreme Court order September 10, 2025 in trans student John Doe lawsuit
adds.summary: South Carolina's 2024-25 and 2025-26 budget laws require students to use bathrooms corresponding to biological sex "at the time of birth," and on September 10, 2025 the U.S. Supreme Court denied South Carolina's August 26, 2025 request to pause a Fourth Circuit order requiring a school district to allow transgender student John Doe to use the boys' bathroom while his equal-protection and federal education anti-discrimination challenge to the law continues, leaving the law unenforceable against Doe during the litigation without ruling on its merits.

adds.title: Medical University of South Carolina cessation of gender-affirming care
adds.summary: South Carolina H4624 took effect May 21, 2024 prohibiting gender transition procedures for persons under 18 and prohibiting direct or indirect use of public funds for gender transition procedures, and because MUSC Health funds are public funds MUSC ceased gender transition services for patients of all ages, stopping new trans patients after August 1, 2024 and transitioning existing patients out by end of January 2025, displacing roughly 500 trans adult patients in the Lowcountry to limited alternative providers while continuing other primary, behavioral and complex care for transgender patients.

adds.title: March 2020 federal judge ruling striking down 1988 anti-gay school classroom law
adds.summary: On March 11, 2020 the U.S. District Court for the District of South Carolina in Gender and Sexuality Alliance v. Spearman declared S.C. Code § 59-32-30(A)(5), the 1988 provision barring any discussion of same-sex relationships in public-school health education except in the context of sexually transmitted diseases with dismissal for violating teachers, unconstitutional under the Fourteenth Amendment Equal Protection Clause for discriminating against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and queer students and barred its enforcement.

adds.title: Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act (federal) / SC hate-crime law gap
adds.summary: As of 26 March 2007, South Carolina had no hate crimes law, so gender identity had no hate-crime protection.
